properties.Chairs: Dr Patricia White, None Sarah Mroz, Dr Rabab Chrifou

content:
Panel 10: Patient and Public Involvement in Palliative Care – round table discussions
This World Café session will bring together people with lived experience, carers, researchers, clinicians, and members NGOs to share perspectives on how patient and public involvement (PPI) can meaningfully shape palliative care research. Through a series of small-group conversations, participants will explore key questions about how we can strengthen PPI, improve collaboration, and ensure that research better reflects the needs and priorities of patients and families across Europe.

properties.Session: EAPC Groups: Current scientific advances in pediatric palliative care: challenging care settings, perinatal palliative care and sedation
properties.Chairs: Dr Jennifer Brandt, Prof Julia Downing, Dr Laure Dombrecht, Prof Erna Michiels

content:
This session will showcase current scientific developments in pediatric palliative care through three focused presentations. 

Creative Strategic Commissioning: Case studies from Austria and Ghana will illustrate innovative models for delivering care in resource-constrained settings, including interdisciplinary approaches, system-wide collaboration, and global action plans.
Perinatal Palliative Care: Speakers will explore the evolution of services across Europe, including antenatal planning, memory-making, and bereavement care. Novel research from Belgium, co-produced with bereaved families, will be presented alongside practical examples of personalized care and interdisciplinary collaboration.
Pediatric Palliative Sedation: Drawing on the first international survey of 348 physicians across five European countries, this segment will examine variations in indications, medication use, and ethical reasoning. The Dutch national guideline, currently the only evidence-based pediatric sedation framework, will be highlighted for its development and implementation.
The session concludes with a discussion on cross-country learning and strategies to improve equity and quality of care.
Aims and learning objectives:
This session aims to present cutting-edge research and practice developments in pediatric palliative care across Europe. Participants will gain insights into:

Innovative strategies for commissioning and delivering children’s palliative care services in resource-constrained settings, including interdisciplinary models and global action plans 

Advances in perinatal palliative care, including antenatal planning, memory-making, and bereavement support for families 

Evidence-based approaches to pediatric palliative sedation, highlighting international survey findings, medication use, and ethical frameworks

Attendees will learn how cultural, societal, and systemic factors shape care and explore practical solutions for improving quality and equity in pediatric palliative care, and will foster cross-country dialogue. 

Speakers:
Dr Jennifer Brandt – Paediatric Intensive Care Physician, University of Vienna (Austria) 

Prof Julia Downing – Chief Executive Officer, International Children’s Palliative Care Network (International) 

Dr Laure Dombrecht – Postdoctoral Researcher, End-of-Life Care Research Group, Vrije Universiteit Brussel & Ghent University (Belgium) 

Dr. Erna Michiels – Pediatric Oncologist, Princess Máxima Center for Pediatric Oncology (Netherlands) Pre-Recorded video presentation.

All speakers are members of the Children and Young People’s (CYP) Reference Group.

properties.Session: EAPC Groups: Patient-Centred Care in the Dying Phase: from Symptoms to Systems
properties.Chairs: Prof Agnes van der Heide, Dr Pilar Barnestein-Fonseca, Dr Antoine Elyn

content:
There are several key challenges to the adequate management of symptoms and needs in the dying phase, including limited education of healthcare professionals in palliative care and emotional discomfort with dying; fragmentation of care and poor communication among care teams, patients, and families; system pressure reducing the time available for holistic, patient-centred care; and misunderstandings about cultural or spiritual needs. In this session, we will discuss the following topics: 

Findings on the prevalence of symptoms and needs of dying patients and their families from the iLIVE project, an 11-country cohort study among 1400 patients in the last phase and life and their families. 

Experiences with a mobile application providing real-time access to patient information, enabling multidisciplinary collaboration in care for dying patients.  

Several examples of how benchmarking can be used in care of the dying, including the potential for international benchmarking.
Multidimensional management of needs in the dying phase is essential for ensuring a dignified and compassionate end-of-life experience for patients and their families. This approach addresses not only physical symptoms but also emotional, psychological, social, and spiritual needs. In this session, we want to discuss the prevalence of symptoms and needs of dying patients across different settings and patient groups; the use of technology in assessing and monitoring symptoms in the dying phase;  and how benchmarking can contribute to optimal management of symptoms and needs. 

Speakers:Prof Agnes van der Heide, Erasmus MC, The Netherlands
Dr Pilar Barnestein Fonseca, Cudeca Institute, Spain
Dr Antoine Pierre Michel Elyn, University Hospital of IcelandAll speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Care for the Dying in collaboration with the International Collaborative of Best Care for the Dying person
